newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Consensus, not coercion, needed at WTO - members.
newsitem.headline: Consensus, not coercion, needed at WTO - members.

text.p: Delegates to a Europe/East Asia economic summit got a taste on Tuesday of what awaits the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting next month -- fiery debate over how best to liberalise trade in developing economies.
Increasing calls for greater access to promising markets in under-developed economies are expected to feature prominently at the WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore.
WTO members should not be required to liberalise their economies beyond their capacity, said Rafidah Aziz, Malaysia's minister of international trade and industry.
"Consensus should not be achieved through the use of political clout," Aziz said.
"People do not agree with each other and then suddenly they are in consensus. Why? Because there is a lot of arm-twisting going on around the back," she said. "That is not consensus."
Aziz won support at the meeting, organised by the World Economic Forum, from Indonesia, which is under fire for its controversial national car programme.
Japan and the United States threatened to take Indonesia to the WTO after the government awarded tax and tariff breaks to a company headed by President Suharto's youngest son.
"All the decisions regarding this WTO matter have to be taken based on consensus, and no member has the legitimate right to enforce their ruling," said Indonesian Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo.

European Commission Vice-President Sir Leon Brittan responded with a reminder that the World Economic Forum was the not the place to ventilate trade disputes, but added a call for Indonesia to bring itself into line with WTO policy.
Brittan also said that there was no question of forcing countries to agree to things, and this is one reason why the WTO negotiating table should be as free from taboos as it is from coercion.
"If there is no risk of your being forced into agreeing to what you don't want, you have no reason to fear a discussion of something," Brittan said.

"I hope we can on that basis, on that double understanding, advance matters. No coercion but no taboos. I really see no justification for saying that a particular subject should not even be the subject of discussion."
Aziz said Malaysia was in favour of removing barriers to trade, but some industries are too young to open them up to international competition.

"One Japanese investor can kill off the entire packaging industry in Malaysia by massive investment. So we say 'Okay, you want to go into packaging, there's an equity condition: not 100 percent,'" she said. "This is not a stand-off, it's not a gap, it's being realistic."
Brittan responded with a challenge for under-developed nations to change their attitude.
"Those who are prepared to strike out and remove obstacles and restrictions and the dead hand of state will gain," he said.
